topics.title: METAR / SPECI decoding
lesson: A METAR is the routine hourly aerodrome weather report. A SPECI is a special report issued between hours when conditions change significantly. This is the Canadian format. Always confirm details against the current Manual of Surface Weather Observations (MANOBS) and your course material.

lesson.formula: METAR CYHZ 261200Z 27015G25KT 15SM -RA BKN020 OVC060 08/06 A2985 RMK SC6AC2 SLP112

list: Station: ICAO identifier (CYHZ is Halifax Stanfield).
Date and time: day of month and UTC time (261200Z is the 26th at 1200 UTC).
Wind: a two-minute mean. Direction in degrees TRUE (to the nearest 10), speed in knots, gusts after G (27015G25KT). 00000KT is calm. VRB means variable.
Visibility: statute miles in Canada, with fractions (1/2SM, 1 1/2SM).
Present weather: intensity (- light, + heavy, no symbol for moderate), then type (RA, SN, FG, BR, TS...).

Cloud: amount and height in hundreds of feet, measured from the aerodrome level at airports (BKN020 is broken at 2,000 ft). Amounts: FEW (more than 0 to 2 oktas), SCT (3 to 4), BKN (5 to 7), OVC (8), SKC (no cloud).
Temperature and dew point in whole degrees C. M means minus (M03/M05 is -3 and -5).
Altimeter: A followed by inches of mercury without the decimal (A2985 is 29.85).

Remarks (RMK): extra detail such as cloud layers in oktas (SC6AC2) and sea level pressure (SLP112 is 1011.2 hPa). To decode: if the three digits start with 7, 8 or 9, put a 9 in front; if they start with 0, 1, 2 or 3, put 10 in front (SLP134 is 1013.4 hPa).
Ceiling: height of the lowest broken or overcast layer, or the vertical visibility when the sky is obscured.
VV003: obscured sky with vertical visibility of 300 ft.

Ceiling: falls below, or rises to equal or exceed, 1500, 1000, 500, 400, 300, 200 or 100 ft (coded 15, 10, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1). The 400, 200 and 100 ft values carry a marker, but MANOBS gives no footnote text for it; the marker points to the bullet on additional limits set by the service provider. Check the service provider's limits for those values.

Visibility: prevailing visibility falls below, or rises to equal or exceed, 3, 1 1/2, 1, 3/4, 1/2 or 1/4 SM. The 3/4 and 1/4 SM values apply only at aerodromes with approved precision approaches, down to the lowest published minima.
Sky condition: a layer aloft is observed below 1,000 ft and none was reported below 1,000 ft in the previous report.
Obstruction to vision: freezing fog begins or ends.
Tornado, waterspout or funnel cloud: observed, reported from a reliable source, or disappears from sight.
Thunderstorm: begins, or ends (15 minutes without thunderstorm activity).

Precipitation: freezing rain, freezing drizzle, ice pellets, rain, rain showers, drizzle, snow, snow showers, snow grains, hail, small hail or snow pellets begin, end or change intensity; ice crystals begin or end. Up to 15 minutes of leeway after precipitation ends.
Temperature (designated sites only, listed in MANOBS Appendix 1): rounded temperature rises 5 C or more from a previous value of 20 C or higher, or falls to a reported value of 2 C or lower.

Wind: two-minute mean speed suddenly at least doubles and exceeds 30 kt; a wind shift occurs (45 degrees or more in under 15 minutes, steady direction, 10 kt or more afterwards); or significant low-level wind shear along the takeoff or approach path at 1,500 ft AGL and below.
Volcanic eruption observed.
Also: on request of a forecast centre or ATS, on the observer's initiative, on notification of an aircraft accident, or on local criteria set by the service provider.

Wind direction: nearest 10 degrees true, three digits, north is 360, calm is 000. Calm: mean speed under 2 kt may be reported calm and 1 kt or less must be (00000KT). Speed in knots, two digits under 100 kt, three at 100 kt and over.

Gusts (G): reported when, in the last 10 minutes, the highest peak is at least 5 kt above the current two-minute mean AND at least 15 kt. A gust is the maximum speed averaged over no more than 5 seconds.

Squall (SQ in present weather): speed rises 15 kt or more over the previous two-minute mean, the peak lasts at least 2 minutes, the one-minute mean reaches at least 20 kt, and speed then drops at least 5 kt. The peak is reported as a gust.

VRB: used when speed is under 3 kt. At higher speeds only if direction varies 180 degrees or more or no single direction can be found. If direction varies 60 degrees or more but under 180 and the mean is 3 kt or more, the two extremes are given clockwise (240V350).

Prevailing visibility: the greatest value common to sectors covering half or more of the horizon circle, observed at eye level (1.5 m). Reportable values: 0 to 3/4 SM in eighths, 1 to 2 1/2 SM in quarters, then 3 to 15 SM in whole miles, then 5 SM steps if markers exist. A value between two reportable values is reported as the lower one. Visibility is not reduced because of darkness alone, and binoculars are not used.

Present weather thresholds: fog (FG) when visibility is 1/2 SM or less; mist (BR) from 5/8 to 6 SM; freezing fog (FZFG) at -0.1 to -30.0 C with visibility 1/2 SM or less; haze, smoke and dust haze when visibility is 6 SM or less; blowing snow, dust and sand when visibility is 6 SM or less and they are the only cause. VC (vicinity) means within 5 SM but not at the station.

Rain intensity by rate of fall: light 2.5 mm/h or less, moderate 2.6 to 7.5, heavy 7.6 or more. Snow, snow grains, snow pellets, drizzle and freezing drizzle by visibility: light 5/8 SM or more; moderate 1/2 or 3/8 SM when alone; heavy 1/4 SM or less when alone. Tornado, waterspout, funnel cloud and thunderstorm carry no intensity.

Sky: amount is the summation of layers at and below that layer. CB and TCU of any amount are always in the remarks, and in the cloud group when they are the predominant type. Heights are in 100 ft steps to 10,000 ft and 1,000 ft steps above. A height between values is reported as the lower value; an amount between values as the greater.

RVR: included only when at least one RVR is 6,000 ft or less or visibility is 1 SM or less. 10-minute mean, range M300 (below 300 ft) to P6000 (above 6,000 ft). Reported in 100 ft steps to 1,200 ft, 200 ft steps to 3,000 ft, 500 ft steps to 6,000 ft.

Timing: a METAR is on the hour; a SPECI is timed at the element that triggered it and should go out within 5 minutes. A correction is marked CCA, then CCB, and so on. A late hourly report carries OBS TAKEN +tt.
Wind shift of 45 degrees or more in under 15 minutes ending at 10 kt or more, or the two-minute mean speed rising 10 kt or more.
Ceiling (lowest BKN or OVC, or vertical visibility) crossing 2,500 ft, 1,000 ft (the IFR/VFR threshold), or the aerodrome alternate minima; or a layer aloft below 1,000 ft where none was reported.
Visibility crossing the no-alternate IFR limit, 1 SM (the IFR/VFR threshold), or the aerodrome alternate minima.

Any change in freezing precipitation intensity; onset or end of hail, freezing fog, freezing rain, rain, snow, thunderstorms or heavy precipitation; onset or end of any precipitation of at least light intensity; onset or end of ice accretion.

lesson.note: METAR and SPECI winds are in degrees true (MANOBS 3.2.1). The exception in MANOBS 12.2.1 is voice communication supporting take-off or landing in the Southern Domestic Airspace, where wind direction is given in tens of degrees magnetic. Always check whether a wind source is true or magnetic before using it for a runway.

terms: Special report issued when conditions change significantly between routine METARs.
Lowest broken or overcast layer, or vertical visibility.
Eighths of the sky covered by cloud.

questions.q: In a METAR, what does 'M03/M05' mean?
questions.e: M indicates a negative value. The first number is temperature, the second is dew point.

questions.q: Wind direction in a METAR is referenced to:
questions.e: MANOBS 3.2.1: wind direction is reported with respect to true north in METAR and SPECI.

questions.q: What does 'VV003' mean?
c: Obscured sky with a vertical visibility of 300 ft
Visibility 3 miles with variable winds at 3 kt
Few clouds at 300 ft above ground with good visibility
Variable wind direction of 003 degrees at low speed
questions.e: VV indicates vertical visibility into an obscured sky, in hundreds of feet.

questions.q: An altimeter group reads A2992. What does that mean?
c: Visibility of 2.9 miles with cloud at 2,000 ft
questions.e: NAV CANADA guide: the letter A prefixes the 4-digit group, which is inches of mercury; A2992 is 29.92 inHg.

questions.q: What defines the ceiling?
c: The lowest broken or overcast layer, or the vertical visibility
The lowest cloud layer reported at any amount, including few
The highest broken or overcast layer reported by the observer
The average height of all the cloud layers in the observation
questions.e: MANOBS 7.2.7: ceiling is the lowest layer aloft reported as broken (BKN) or overcast (OVC), or the vertical visibility (VV). FEW and SCT layers do not constitute a ceiling.

questions.q: In a METAR, what does the group 'BKN012' mean?
c: Broken cloud layer with base at 1,200 ft
Broken cloud layer with base at 12,000 ft
questions.e: Heights are in hundreds of feet. At airports they are measured from the official aerodrome level (MANOBS 7.3.1). 012 = 1,200 ft.

questions.q: What does '18015G25KT' report?
c: Wind from 180 degrees at 15 kt, gusting 25 kt
Wind from 150 degrees at 18 kt, gusting 25 kt
Wind from 180 degrees at 25 kt, gusting 15 kt
questions.e: Direction (3 digits), speed (2 digits), G, gust, then unit.

questions.q: A METAR shows temperature/dew point group '03/M01'. What are the values?
questions.e: The M prefix means minus.

questions.q: Which group in a METAR shows the altimeter setting in inches of mercury?
questions.e: In Canada and the US, altimeter is reported as A followed by four digits.

questions.q: What does 'VRB05KT' indicate?
c: Wind from 050 degrees at 5 kt, steady
Calm winds with no measurable speed
Wind from the north at 5 kt, steady
questions.e: VRB is used for light, variable winds.

questions.q: A SPECI is issued when:
c: Significant changes meet specified criteria between routine reports
Every hour on the hour, whatever the weather at the station, under normal operating conditions
Only at midnight, when the observer changes shift
Only when winds exceed 50 kt at the observing site, as agreed locally with the data user
questions.e: SPECI reports are special reports after significant changes.

questions.q: A SPECI is required when the prevailing visibility decreases to less than which of these values?
questions.e: MANOBS 11.2.3.4: the first visibility value is 3 mi., then 1 1/2, 1, 3/4, 1/2 and 1/4.

questions.q: Which ceiling value, in feet, is a SPECI criterion?
How long after thunderstorm activity stops is a SPECI required for the end of the thunderstorm?
questions.e: MANOBS 11.2.3.6: the thunderstorm ends when 15 minutes pass without thunderstorm activity.

questions.q: Which temperature change prompts a SPECI at a designated site?
c: A fall to a reported 2 C or lower
A fall of 1 C in an hour
A rise to any value above 0 C
A rise of 2 C from a previous 10 C
questions.e: MANOBS 11.2.3.8: a decrease to 2 C or lower, or a rise of 5 C or more from a previous value of 20 C or higher.

questions.q: What wind change meets the SPECI criterion for speed?
c: Two-minute mean at least doubles and exceeds 30 kt
Any gust above 15 kt in the last ten minutes
Speed rises by 5 kt within a ten-minute period
Speed exceeds 20 kt for a full minute or more
questions.e: MANOBS 11.2.3.9.

questions.q: Which of these does a SPECI require when it begins or ends?
questions.e: MANOBS 11.2.3.2: obstruction to vision criterion is freezing fog beginning or ending.

questions.q: A two-minute mean wind of 1 kt is reported as:
questions.e: MANOBS 3.2.4: a mean wind of 1 kt or less shall be reported as calm.

questions.q: Which pair of conditions must both be met in the last 10 minutes to report gusts?
c: Peak at least 5 kt above the two-minute mean and at least 15 kt
Peak at least 10 kt above the mean and at least 20 kt, unless a supervisor directs otherwise
Peak at least 3 kt above the mean and at least 10 kt
Peak at least 15 kt above the mean and at least 25 kt, for the period covered by the product
questions.e: MANOBS 3.3.1: the highest peak is at least 5 kt higher than the current two-minute average and at least 15 kt.

questions.q: VRB is used for wind direction when the speed is:
questions.e: MANOBS 3.3.4: VRB when speed is less than 3 kt. At higher speeds only if the variation is 180 degrees or more or no single direction can be determined.

questions.q: Wind direction varies between 240 and 350 degrees over 10 minutes with a mean of 8 kt. How is it reported?
c: VRB08KT, because the direction is variable
questions.e: MANOBS 3.3.5: a variation of 60 degrees or more but under 180, with a mean of 3 kt or more, is reported as the two extreme directions in clockwise order.

questions.q: The observed visibility falls between two reportable values. Which is reported?
questions.e: MANOBS 4.5.1.1: the lower value shall be reported.

questions.q: What is the prevailing visibility?
c: The greatest value common to sectors covering half or more of the horizon circle
The lowest visibility seen in any direction around the station, as set out in the governing publication
The average of the visibility in all directions around the station, as set out in the governing publication
The visibility in the direction of the active runway only
questions.e: MANOBS 4.2: the maximum visibility value common to sectors comprising one-half or more of the horizon circle.

questions.q: Mist (BR) is reported when the prevailing visibility is:
questions.e: MANOBS 6.7.1.3. Fog (FG) is reported at 1/2 SM or less (6.7.1.1).

questions.q: Freezing fog (FZFG) is reported at temperatures of:
c: -0.1 to -30.0 C with visibility 1/2 SM or less
Below 0 C with visibility 3 SM or less
0 to 5 C with visibility 1/2 SM or less, based on the most recent routine report
Any temperature with visibility under 1 SM, as set out in the governing publication
questions.e: MANOBS 6.7.1.2. Below -30.0 C it needs clear physical evidence of ice accretion from fog.

questions.q: What rate of fall defines heavy rain in a Canadian METAR?
questions.e: MANOBS 6.6.2.5.2: light 2.5 mm/h or less, moderate 2.6 to 7.5, heavy 7.6 or more.

questions.q: The vicinity qualifier VC is used for phenomena observed:
c: Within 5 SM but not at the station
Within 25 SM of the station, in any direction
Anywhere in sight of the observer
At the station only, never beyond it
questions.e: MANOBS 6.7.1.8: within 5 mi. or less but not occurring at the point of observation.

questions.q: Cumulonimbus or towering cumulus observed at any amount must:
c: Always be reported in the remarks
Be reported only if the cloud is overhead
Be reported only when the sky is BKN or OVC
Be left out of the METAR if the amount is small
questions.e: MANOBS 7.3 item 5: CB and TCU of any amount shall always be reported in the remark.

questions.q: The RVR group is included in a METAR when at least one RVR is:
c: 6,000 ft or less, or visibility is 1 SM or less
Under 1,000 ft only, with no visibility test
Below 3,000 ft, or visibility is 3 SM or less
Under 600 ft, or visibility is 1/4 SM or less
questions.e: MANOBS 5.2: included when at least one RVR reports 6 000 ft or less, or prevailing visibility is 1 mi. or less.

questions.q: How is the first correction to a METAR marked?
questions.e: MANOBS 11.2.2.5: CC followed by an incrementing letter, CCA for the first correction, CCB for the second.

sources: MANOBS 8th ed. Amendment 3: 2.5 (METAR and SPECI), 3.2.1 (wind, two-minute mean, true), 4.5.1 (visibility in SM), 7.2.7 (ceiling), 7.3.1 (cloud reference level)
NAV CANADA Aviation Weather Services Guide (2017): METAR decode, oktas ranges, M prefix, A group in inHg, intensity qualifiers, SLP decoding
Transport Canada AIM MET 1.2.1: METARs hourly on the hour
MANOBS 8th ed. Amendment 3 (full PDF): 11.2.3.1 to 11.2.3.11 (SPECI criteria), 3.3.3 (wind shift), 8.3 and 9.2 (temperature and QNH format)

MANOBS 8th ed. Am. 3 (full PDF): 2.8 to 2.9 (times, SPECI timing), 3.2 to 3.3 (wind), 4.2 and 4.5 (visibility), 5.2 (RVR), 6.6 to 6.7 (intensity, fog, mist, VC), 7.3 (sky), 11.2.2 (coding), 12.2.1 (magnetic wind for voice), 12.2.7 (AUTO SPECI)

The precision-approach note is attached only to the 3/4 and 1/4 SM visibility values. Gap in the source; confirm with ECCC/NAV CANADA.

topics.title: TAF decoding and amendment criteria
lesson: A TAF is the forecaster's best judgment of the most probable weather at an aerodrome and its most probable time of occurrence (MANAIR 2.1). It relates to conditions for flight operations within six statute miles (roughly five nautical miles) of the centre of the runway complex, depending on local terrain. Certain phenomena expected in the vicinity are also included. All times are UTC.

lesson.formula:
TAF CYHZ 261140Z 2612/2712 27012KT P6SM FEW040 SCT100
  FM261800 29015G25KT P6SM SCT040
  BECMG 2700/2702 31008KT
  TEMPO 2703/2706 3SM -SHRA BKN015

list: Issue time (261140Z) is when the forecast is released. A TAF should be sent as close as possible to, and no later than, 20 minutes before its period of validity begins.

Valid period 2612/2712: from 1200 UTC on the 26th to 1200 UTC on the 27th. A TAF is valid from the moment it is issued until it is amended, replaced by the next TAF, or its period ends. A new TAF cancels the previous one.
TAFs are normally scheduled six hours after the previous issue and never more than seven hours after.

Updated TAFs (requested by NAV CANADA for major aerodromes, usually with 24 or 30 hour TAFs) are issued about three hours after each regular TAF. They replace the previous TAF without extending its validity.
Airports without 24-hour observing need two consecutive hourly observations before issuing. With fewer, a nil TAF is issued (TAF CYTS 051640Z NIL, with NO OBS or INSUFFICIENT OBS in remarks).
Every TAF describes at least wind, visibility, weather and cloud.

Wind: direction to the nearest 10 degrees true, speed in knots. A gust group is added only when the maximum is forecast to exceed the mean by 10 kt or more (32020G30KT). VRB is normally used only at 3 kt or less (or in strong convective activity). North 20 kt is 36020KT, calm is 00000KT, 100 kt or more uses three digits.

Low level wind shear (WSh x h x h x /dddffKT): non-convective shear within 1,500 ft AGL, included when the forecaster has strong evidence. Guidelines: vector difference over 25 kt within 500 ft, over 40 kt within 1,000 ft, over 50 kt within 1,500 ft, or a pilot report of a 20 kt or greater airspeed change within 1,500 ft. The group is not part of the international code (Canada filed a difference with ICAO).
Visibility is in statute miles: eighths to 3/4 SM, quarters to 2 1/2 SM, then 3, 4, 5, 6 SM, then P6SM for more than 6 SM. Unlike a METAR, a TAF never goes above P6SM.

Obscurations (BR, FG, HZ, FU and so on) are forecast whenever visibility is expected to be 6 SM or less; volcanic ash is always forecast. In a TAF, FG means visibility under 5/8 SM and BR means 5/8 SM or more.

Up to three weather groups. The group is omitted if no significant weather is expected. DZ and IC cannot be combined with other precipitation; RA, SN, SG, PL, GR and GS can (SNRA, PLSN). MI, BC and PR are used only with FG and only with P6SM visibility.

VC is used for FG, TS, SH, DS, SS, FC, PO, BL phenomena and VA expected 6 to 10 SM from the centre of the runway complex. At the four hubs (CYYZ, CYVR, CYUL, CYYC) VCTS can describe organized storms within about 45 SM of the terminal area.

Cloud: amounts SKC, FEW, SCT, BKN, OVC are cumulative. A maximum of three significant layers, except CB, which is always forecast when expected. TCU and ACC are never forecast. Heights are in hundreds of feet above ground: 100 ft steps to 1,500 ft, 500 ft steps to 3,000 ft, 1,000 ft steps above. VV is used for an obscured sky; SKC replaces cloud after a change if cloud is no longer expected.

When a significant change is forecast (one that would need an amendment), the whole weather group is repeated, including the visibility and unchanged weather such as BR. If an element is unchanged after BECMG or TEMPO, it is left out.

FM (from): a permanent change, typically over an hour or less, written FM followed by day, hour and minute (FM300130). All forecast elements are restated and it supersedes everything before it. Forecasters are encouraged to use FM rather than BECMG, and minutes are encouraged for timing precision.

BECMG (becoming): a gradual, permanent change that normally lasts no more than 2 hours and never more than 4 (BECMG 2906/2908). Keep it for one or at most two changing elements; use FM when more than two change. Normally one BECMG per part period, at most two when only one element changes at a time.

TEMPO (temporary): a fluctuation expected to last less than one hour each time and, if recurring, to cover no more than half of the stated period (TEMPO 1306/1312). Only changed elements are listed. Wind can be included (example: TEMPO 1520/1523 VRB25G45KT 1SM TSRAGS). Normally one TEMPO per part period, at most two with no BECMG or PROB, one element each and no overlap.

PROB30 or PROB40: the only probabilities allowed. It gives the probability that the alternative value occurs. Under 30% is not forecast; 50% or more is written as BECMG, TEMPO or FM. PROB is used for thunderstorms and associated phenomena, freezing precipitation, ice pellets, snow grains, low level wind shear, and ceiling or visibility thresholds important to aircraft. One PROB per part period. PROB30 TEMPO and PROB BECMG are not allowed.
Thunderstorm wording (MANAIR Table 3): a TSRA in the main body means 60 to 100% at the airport, TEMPO TSRA 40 to 60%, PROB40 TSRA 40%, PROB30 TSRA 30%, TEMPO VCTS about 20%.
NSW (no significant weather) replaces the weather group after TEMPO or BECMG when significant weather ends. It is not used in the initial period.

An amended TAF is marked TAF AMD and covers the rest of the original validity. The forecaster has the responsibility and authority to amend, and should amend proactively when the TAF no longer represents existing or expected weather. A correction is handled as an amendment.

Category rule: amend when actual or expected conditions fall in a different weather category from the forecast. The category is set by the lower of ceiling or visibility. Thresholds: ceiling 2,500 ft and visibility 6 SM; ceiling 1,000 ft and visibility 3 SM (VFR/IFR); the aerodrome's alternate limits; its IFR approach limits; and any additional limits from other responsible parties (published in MANAIR Appendix A). Deteriorating: either ceiling or visibility crossing is enough. Improving: both must cross.
No amendment is needed for ceiling or visibility changes when forecast and observed values are both below the lowest landing minima, provided those minima are not higher than 1,000 ft / 3 SM.

Always amend, whatever the visibility or duration, for thunderstorms, hail, tornado, funnel cloud or waterspout; freezing precipitation, freezing fog, ice pellets or snow grains; sandstorm, dust storm or squalls, whenever not forecast or no longer expected. Volcanic ash always.

Rain, snow, snow pellets, ice crystals or drizzle: amend only if visibility drops under 6 SM (or was forecast under 6 SM and is no longer expected). Obscurations and blowing snow likewise: only if visibility is under 6 SM.

Wind: amend when the observed speed is double or half the forecast and either value is over 15 kt, or the difference is 20 kt or more; or when the observed direction differs by 45 degrees or more at speeds over 15 kt. Amend for low level wind shear not forecast, or forecast and no longer expected.

Cancellation: an existing TAF is cancelled by an amendment (CNL, with the same validity as the last TAF and the reason in remarks) when two consecutive hourly observations are missing or a critical AWOS element is missing or wrong for two hours and cannot be inferred. Service is reinstated after one VFR observation or two consecutive below-VFR observations.

lesson.note: When decoding, read the base forecast first, then apply each change group in order. A validity period that ends at midnight UTC is coded 24 (2912/2924); one that begins at midnight is coded 00 (3000/3018). For alternate planning, a TAF with BECMG or TEMPO must meet alternate minima, while PROB conditions need only meet landing minima (NAV CANADA guide).

terms: From: a permanent change with a new complete forecast from the stated time.
Becoming: gradual permanent change, normally up to 2 hours and never over 4.
Temporary: fluctuations under one hour at a time, no more than half the period in total.
Probability of the alternative condition. No other probability values are allowed.
Visibility more than 6 statute miles. The highest value a TAF uses.
No significant weather: replaces the weather group when it ends after a change group.
Low level wind shear group, non-convective, within 1,500 ft AGL.

questions.q: What does an FM group in a TAF indicate?
c: A rapid change with a new complete forecast from the stated time
A gradual change that develops slowly during the stated period
A short-lived fluctuation that returns to the previous conditions
A probability forecast that applies for the next six hours only
questions.e: FM replaces all previous conditions starting at the stated time.

questions.q: What does BECMG mean?
c: A gradual change during the stated period
A sudden change that replaces all earlier groups
A brief fluctuation lasting under an hour each time
A probability of change between thirty and forty percent
questions.e: MANAIR 2.6.16.2: a gradual, permanent change; the period normally does not exceed two hours and never exceeds four.

questions.q: What does TEMPO indicate?
c: Temporary fluctuations, each lasting less than an hour
A permanent change that replaces the main forecast
A change that always lasts more than 2 hours at a time
A reduction in visibility only, never in cloud or wind
questions.e: MANAIR 2.6.15: TEMPO is used when the change lasts less than one hour each time and, if recurring, covers no more than half of the stated period.

questions.q: What does P6SM mean in a TAF?
c: Visibility less than 6 statute miles in precipitation
A six percent probability of reduced visibility
Pressure falling six hectopascals in the next hour
questions.e: P means plus, so more than 6 statute miles.

questions.q: What area does a TAF cover?
c: The area within about 5 NM of the aerodrome
The entire province in which the aerodrome is located
An area of about 100 NM around the aerodrome
Only the runway surface and its immediate approach lights
questions.e: MANAIR 2.1: conditions for flight operations within six statute miles (roughly five nautical miles) of the centre of the runway complex, depending on local terrain.

questions.q: A TAF valid period of '2412/2512' covers:
c: 1200 UTC on the 24th to 1200 UTC on the 25th
2400 UTC on the 12th to 2500 UTC on the 12th
1200 UTC on the 12th to 1200 UTC on the 25th
questions.e: The format is DDHH/DDHH in UTC. A period ending at midnight UTC is coded 24 (for example 2912/2924).

questions.q: What does 'TEMPO' in a TAF indicate?
c: Temporary fluctuations lasting less than one hour at a time, under half the period
A permanent change that lasts for the rest of the valid period, as agreed locally with the data user
A change with a 50% probability of occurring in the period
The cancellation of the forecast and its replacement by a new one, based on the most recent routine report
questions.e: MANAIR 2.6.15: under one hour each time and no more than half the period in total.

questions.q: What does 'BECMG' mean?
c: A gradual change to new conditions
A temporary change lasting less than an hour at a time
A calm period with winds below 3 kt at the airport
An amendment to the forecast issued after a major change
questions.e: MANAIR 2.6.16.2: a gradual, permanent change; the period normally does not exceed two hours and never exceeds four.

questions.q: 'PROB30' in a TAF signals:
c: A 30% probability of the stated conditions
A 30-minute delay before the change in conditions begins
A wind speed of 30 kt in the stated period
A visibility of 30 km in the stated period
questions.e: NAV CANADA guide: PROB30 or PROB40 is the probability that the condition occurs during the period, not the fraction of time it lasts.

questions.q: An amendment (AMD) is issued when:
c: Forecast conditions no longer represent expected weather
At the start of each new valid period in the forecast
At random times chosen by the forecaster on shift
Only when winds at the airport are calm for an hour
questions.e: MANAIR 2.9: a TAF is amended when conditions are no longer representative of actual or expected weather, using the category and phenomenon criteria in 2.9.5.

questions.q: TAF cloud and visibility values are expressed:
c: In a similar manner to METAR
In metres and kilometres, unlike the METAR format
In kilometres only, with cloud in metres above sea level
In inches of mercury for pressure and feet for visibility
questions.e: Same style of codes as METAR, but a TAF visibility tops out at P6SM and a TAF forecasts at most three cloud layers plus CB (MANAIR 2.6.10 and 2.6.13).

questions.q: What is the longest a BECMG period may last?

topics.title: Surface analysis and prognostic charts
lesson: A surface analysis chart shows the observed pattern of pressure, fronts and weather at a fixed time. A prognostic chart ('prog') shows the forecast pattern at a future time.

list: Isobars: lines of equal sea level pressure, analysed at 4 hPa intervals from a 1000 hPa reference value. The national surface analysis is produced four times a day, valid 00, 06, 12 and 18 UTC. Tight spacing means strong winds. Labels traditionally show only the last two digits (NOAA JetStream examples: 24 is 1024 hPa, 08 is 1008, 92 is 992; so 96 is 996 and 04 is 1004).
H and L: high and low centres, with central pressure.

Fronts (MANAIR GFA symbols): cold front is blue with triangles; warm front is red with semicircles; stationary front alternates a red semicircle and a blue triangle on opposite sides. The GFA also uses a trowal (blue dashes with red ticks) and upper fronts, drawn hollow. Check the legend on any other chart.
Troughs: on the GFA a surface trough is a dashed magenta line and an upper trough is a double dashed magenta line. Troughs and ridges are lines of curvature of the isobars.
Station models: plotted observations at each station.
Temperature: upper left. Dew point: lower left.

Pressure: upper right, mean sea level pressure in tenths of hPa with the decimal point and the leading 9 or 10 dropped. Add the 9 or 10 that gives a value closest to 1000 (998 is 999.8; 024 is 1002.4).
Pressure tendency: centre right. A number (3-hour change in tenths of hPa) and a trend symbol.
Sky cover: the circle at the centre, filled by the amount of cloud cover (eighths).

Visibility and present weather: second row, left side. Present weather is plotted only when precipitation or reduced visibility is occurring. Past weather (previous 6 hours, excluding the last hour): lower right.
Wind: lines extend from the sky cover circle, the longest pointing toward where the wind comes from. Full barb 10 kt, half barb 5 kt, pennant (flag) 50 kt. A circle alone is calm.
Source note: this layout is the NOAA (US) plot. The US plots temperature in F; Canadian charts use C. The Canadian layout was not found in a Canadian source.

lesson: Isobar spacing gives a rough guide to wind speed. Winds blow roughly parallel to the isobars, slightly across them toward lower pressure near the surface. Low pressure on the left in the Northern Hemisphere. NAV CANADA guide: winds tend to veer and increase with altitude, and above about 3,000 ft AGL they blow roughly parallel to the isobars. Fronts advance in the direction of the barbs or semicircles. A front that is not advancing is quasi-stationary. A trowal is a trough of warm air aloft.

list: Surface analysis (mean sea level pressure) is posted four times daily for 00, 06, 12 and 18 UTC, in two versions: Preliminary (Canadian coverage) and Complete (Northern Hemispheric coverage).
Analyses are built from reports by hundreds of stations, ships and aircraft in Canada, the US and elsewhere, received at the CMC.

Notice on the page: the Surface Analysis (Preliminary, Canadian coverage), Upper Air Analysis, Snow Depth, Sea Surface Temperature and Sea Ice Cover map products are to be decommissioned by the end of 2026. ECCC points users to MSC AniMet, which draws maps from MSC open data.
Low or tropical depression: L with central pressure. High: H with central pressure.
Movement: an arrow with the speed in knots in a box.
Tropical cyclone: a storm symbol and a hurricane symbol (filled), plus a post-tropical symbol (L).
Organized cloud: brown scalloped outline. Obstruction to vision: dashed orange outline.
Continuous precipitation: solid green (rain, drizzle, snow) or solid red (freezing rain, freezing drizzle, ice pellets), stippled.
Intermittent precipitation or showers: dashed green or dashed red, hatched.
Icing: blue outline, stippled (denser for severe). Turbulence: red outline, hatched; lower-level and higher-level hatch directions differ, and severe is denser.
Freezing level: dashed contour with boxed height (SFC, 25, 50). AFL marks an above-freezing layer, shown with its top over its base.
Surface wind is shown with a barb and a boxed gust (G60). A low-level jet is shown with arrows and a box (L LVL JET 50KT).
Volcano and radioactive release have their own symbols.

lesson.note: A prog is a model-based forecast reviewed by a forecaster. Compare the prog with the latest analysis to check how well the model captured the current situation.

topics.title: Upper-air charts (850, 700, 500, 250 hPa)
lesson: Upper-air charts are drawn for constant pressure levels, prepared twice daily at 00 and 12 UTC. They show geopotential height (the height at which that pressure is found), temperature, dew point depression and wind. Data come from radiosonde balloons, supplemented by aircraft reports and, in remote regions, satellite-derived winds (NAV CANADA guide).

list: 850 hPa (about 1,500 m, 5,000 ft ASL): low-level temperature and moisture. Warm and cold advection, the 0 C line, low-level jets, and rain versus snow guidance.
700 hPa (about 3,000 m, 10,000 ft ASL): mid-level moisture and ascent. Cloud layers, steering of low-level systems, and the capping inversion for convection.
500 hPa (about 5,500 m, 18,000 ft ASL): the main steering level. Troughs, ridges, vorticity, and cut-off lows. Closely spaced contours mean strong winds.
250 hPa (about 10,400 m, 34,000 ft ASL) and nearby 300 hPa (about 9,000 m): jet streams, upper divergence, tropopause-level features. Isotachs show wind speed maxima.
250 hPa: geopotential height and wind velocity.
500 hPa: geopotential height and 1000-500 hPa thickness.
700 hPa: geopotential height, temperature and dew point depression.
850 hPa: geopotential height and temperature.
These ECCC map products are listed for decommissioning by the end of 2026 (MSC AniMet is the suggested replacement).

Each chart is for one pressure level. What varies is the height of that level: it is lower where the air is cold and dense and higher where it is warm. Contours join points of equal height and are analysed like isobars: the closer the spacing, the stronger the wind.
Height contours (in decametres, dam). Flow is parallel to the contours with low heights on the left in the Northern Hemisphere.
Wind crossing isotherms: if wind blows from warm toward cold, there is warm advection. Cold toward warm is cold advection.
Dew point depression (temperature minus dew point): a small value (for example 3 C or less) means moist, probably cloud.
Closely spaced contours mean strong wind, and jets appear where speeds are highest.

lesson.note: Use 850 for temperature and precipitation type, 700 for moisture and ascent, 500 for the large-scale pattern, and 250 for the jet.

terms: Height of a pressure surface above sea level, adjusted for gravity variations.

topics.title: Numerical weather prediction (GEM, GFS, ECMWF) and limitations
lesson: Numerical weather prediction (NWP) solves the equations of fluid motion and thermodynamics on a grid to forecast the atmosphere. Forecasters use model output as guidance, not as the final answer.

list: GEM (Global Environmental Multiscale model): ECCC's atmospheric model. The Global Deterministic Prediction System (GDPS) runs at about 15 km out to 10 days, twice a day. The High Resolution Deterministic Prediction System (HRDPS Continental) runs at about 2.5 km over most of Canada out to 48 hours, up to four times a day.
GFS: the US National Weather Service global model.
ECMWF: the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts. Widely regarded as one of the most skillful global models.

lesson: Resolutions and run schedules change as models are upgraded. The ECCC figures above were read from ECCC's data catalogue on 2026-10-26. Check the current documentation.

list: Chaos: tiny errors in the starting state grow over time, so forecast skill falls with lead time. Little skill is expected beyond about two weeks.
Parameterization: processes smaller than the grid (convection, cloud microphysics, turbulence) are approximated.
Resolution: coarse models smooth out small features. A high-resolution model can resolve thunderstorms, terrain effects and sea breezes better, but it can also be wrong in more detail.
Initial conditions: observations are limited, especially over oceans.

lesson: An ensemble runs the model many times with slightly different starting conditions or physics. The spread among members shows uncertainty. Tight agreement means higher confidence. Large spread means low confidence and several possible outcomes.

lesson.note: Never rely on one model run. Compare models, check trends from run to run, and use ensembles to judge confidence.

terms: Representation of processes too small to resolve on the model grid.
Set of forecasts from slightly different starting conditions or physics.

topics.title: Forecast verification and persistence
lesson: Verification checks how good forecasts are. It guides improvement and shows when to trust or discount a source.

list: Persistence: assume tomorrow will be like today. Very hard to beat for the first few hours in some elements, and a useful baseline.
Climatology: use the long-term average for the date. A baseline for longer ranges.

lesson.h: Yes/no event scores (from a contingency table)

list: Hits: event forecast and occurred. Misses: not forecast but occurred. False alarms: forecast but did not occur. Correct negatives: neither.
Probability of detection (POD) = hits / (hits + misses).
False alarm ratio (FAR) = false alarms / (hits + false alarms).
Critical success index (CSI) = hits / (hits + misses + false alarms).
Bias: average error. Shows consistent over or under forecasting.
Mean absolute error (MAE) and root mean square error (RMSE): size of typical errors. RMSE penalizes big misses more.

lesson.formula: Skill = (score - reference score) / (perfect score - reference score)

lesson: A positive skill score means the forecast beat the reference. Zero means no better. Negative means worse.
For rare events, a forecast of 'no' every day is right most of the time but has no use. Use POD, FAR and CSI for rare events.

lesson.note: Verify against what matters to the user: thresholds like ceiling below 1,000 ft, not just average temperature error.

terms: Forecast that current conditions will continue.

Weather is random, so no forecast beats chance
Weather always changes within the next six hours

questions.q: A forecast has 40 hits, 10 misses and 20 false alarms. What is the probability of detection (POD)?
questions.e: POD = hits / (hits + misses) = 40/50 = 0.80.

questions.q: Using hits 40, misses 10, false alarms 20, what is the false alarm ratio (FAR)?
questions.e: FAR = false alarms / (hits + false alarms) = 20/60 = 0.33.

questions.q: Using hits 40, misses 10, false alarms 20, what is the critical success index (CSI)?
questions.e: CSI = hits / (hits + misses + false alarms) = 40/70 = 0.57.

topics.title: GFA, SIGMET, AIRMET and winds aloft (FB)
lesson: These are the main Canadian aviation hazard products. The source is MANAIR (Manual of Standards and Procedures for Aviation Weather Forecasts, ECCC).

list: Six charts: clouds and weather, and icing/turbulence/freezing level, each at T+0, T+6 and T+12 hours. The last clouds and weather chart also has a 12-hour IFR outlook (hours 12 to 24).
Issued at 2330, 0530, 1130 and 1730 UTC, valid 00, 06, 12 and 18 UTC. Seven domains. Covers the surface to 24,000 ft.
Units: heights ASL unless noted, ceilings AGL. Wind direction is true. Visibility in SM. Time in UTC.
Standard phrases: HGTS ASL UNLS NOTED / CB TCU AND ACC IMPLY SIG TURB AND ICE / CB IMPLIES L LVL WS.
Organized BKN or OVC cloud is enclosed in a brown scalloped line. Cirrus is not mentioned.
Layers less than 2,000 ft apart are combined (LYRS). Layers 2,000 ft or more apart are each stated.
Convective clouds (CU, TCU, ACC, CB) are always indicated, with tops even above 24,000 ft.
Convective qualifiers: ISOL 25% or less, OCNL over 25% to 50%, FRQ over 50%. Non-convective: LCA 25% or less, PTCHY over 25% to 50%, XTNSV over 50%.
Visibility is always given; over 6 SM is P6SM. Areas of 6 SM or less are enclosed by a dashed orange line.
Continuous precipitation: solid green line, stippled; red for freezing precipitation. Convective or intermittent: dashed green, hatched.
Isobars: solid black, every 4 hPa from 1000 hPa (this chart only).
Strong winds: wind barbs where mean wind is 20 kt or more. Gusts are shown when 10 kt or more above the mean.
Synoptic features moving 5 kt or more get an arrow and speed. Slower is STNR.

lesson.h: GFA icing, turbulence and freezing level chart

lesson: Moderate and severe non-convective icing (blue) and turbulence (red), with base and top as a fraction (top over base, hundreds of feet ASL). Freezing level is a dashed contour. See the icing and turbulence topics.

list: Types: WS (TS, TURB, ICE, MTW, L LVL WS, DS, SS, RDOACT CLD), WV (volcanic ash), WC (tropical cyclone). Covers up to FL600.

One phenomenon per SIGMET. Criteria: FRQ or SQL TS (hail and tornado/waterspout as needed); SEV TURB; SEV ICE (with or without FZRA); SEV MTW; SEV L LVL WS; HVY DS; HVY SS; RDOACT CLD; VA; TC with 10-minute mean surface wind of 34 kt (63 km/h) or more.
WS: valid 4 hours, issued up to 4 hours ahead, updated every 4 hours. WV and WC: valid 6 hours, issued up to 12 hours ahead, updated every 6 hours.
OBS means a recent observation (normally within 2 hours, never more than 3). FCST means the phenomenon is expected or strongly indicated by guidance.
A forecast-event SIGMET is issued only for first appearance in Canadian airspace. A phenomenon moving between Canadian FIRs is treated as ongoing.
Must be cancelled when the phenomenon ends or is no longer expected. A SIGMET is issued regardless of whether it is in the GFA.
For specified phenomena up to FL240 that are NOT already in the GFA.

Phenomena: widespread surface wind over 30 kt; widespread visibility under 3 SM and/or BKN or OVC below 1,000 ft AGL; ISOL or OCNL TS (TCU also if FRQ); MOD TURB; MOD ICE; MOD MTW. Widespread means 50% or more of the area.
Valid 4 hours, issued up to 4 hours ahead, updated every 4 hours. It does not cancel itself at the end of validity.
Cancel when the phenomenon ends, when it strengthens to SIGMET criteria, or when a new GFA includes it.
Once issued, a SIGMET or AIRMET automatically amends the current GFA.
Model-based, issued four times daily from 00, 06, 12 and 18 UTC data. FBCN31, FBCN33 and FBCN35 are the 6, 12 and 24 hour forecasts.
Levels: 3,000 (omitted when terrain is above 1,500 ft), 6,000, 9,000, 12,000 and 18,000 ft ASL. No temperature at 3,000 ft. The US NWS issues 24,000 to 53,000 ft.
Code ddfftt: direction in tens of degrees true, speed in knots, temperature in degrees C.
100 to 199 kt: subtract 100 from the speed and add 50 to the direction digits (240 deg at 130 kt = 7430). Over 199 kt is coded as 199. Under 5 kt is 9900.
Temperature sign is shown below 24,000 ft; above that, temperatures are negative and no sign is written.
A GFA is corrected for: unforecast weather not requiring an AIRMET, forecast weather that fails to occur, or a significant error.

Unforecast phenomena that justify correction include: widespread BKN or OVC with base between 1,000 and 5,000 ft AGL; widespread visibility between 3 and 6 SM; widespread mean surface wind of 20 to 30 kt, or peak gust of 30 kt or more.
GFA domains are numbered GFACN31 to GFACN37. GFACN33 is Ontario-Quebec. GFACN37 (the far north) is on request only.

Flight categories used in the GFA IFR outlook: IFR is ceiling under 1,000 ft AGL or visibility under 3 SM. MVFR is ceiling 1,000 to 3,000 ft AGL or visibility 3 to 5 SM. VFR is ceiling above 3,000 ft AGL and visibility above 5 SM.
The IFR outlook covers an additional 12 hours beyond the GFA valid period.
Surface-based layers use OBSCD: LCL OBSCD CIG 3-5 AGL means local obscured ceilings between 300 and 500 ft AGL.
Obstructions to vision are mentioned only when visibility is forecast to be 6 SM or less. Visibility may be given as a range, for example 2-4 SM -SHRA.
Dashed orange encloses obscuring phenomena other than precipitation (for example haze). Dashed red encloses intermittent freezing precipitation.
Turbulence depiction: red outline; light positive cross-hatching is moderate low-level, dense positive is severe low-level, light negative is moderate high-level, dense negative is severe high-level.
Freezing level contours are dashed, starting at SFC and at 2,500 ft intervals (the guide describes them as red; MANAIR text says only 'dashed').

lesson.h: Where the NAV CANADA guide and MANAIR differ

list: Surface wind: the guide says wind is included only if 20 kt or more, or gusts to 30 kt or more. MANAIR 4.9.1.5 says barbs for mean wind of 20 kt or more, with gusts shown when 10 kt or more above the mean. MANAIR (2024) is the newer standard.

Cloud layers: the guide says summation amount is not used and each organized layer is considered individually. MANAIR says layers less than 2,000 ft apart are combined and marked LYRS. MANAIR is the newer standard.
Slow-moving fronts: the guide's example uses QS (quasi-stationary) when movement is under 5 kt; MANAIR uses STNR.
Turbulence cause labels: the guide lists MECH, LLWS, LEE WV, LLJ, CAT; MANAIR lists MECH, L LVL WS, MTW (the 2026 AIM uses LEE WV), L LVL JET, CAT.

lesson.h: Significant weather (Sig Wx) prognostic charts (MANAIR Ch. 7, NAV CANADA guide)

list: Purpose: Sig Wx charts show the most probable forecast conditions over large areas and are designed mainly for preflight planning. The CMACs issue two: the Canadian chart (CAN SIG WX) and the North Atlantic chart (NAT SIG WX). The GFA is a separate product.

CAN SIG WX (MANAIR 7.3.1): mid-levels, 700 to 400 hPa (FL100 to FL240). Issued four times a day at about 0210, 0815, 1425 and 1940 UTC, valid 12, 18, 00 and 06 UTC (about 10 hours ahead). Covers the seven GFA domains.

NAT SIG WX (MANAIR 7.3.2): surface to 400 hPa (surface to FL240). Valid 00 and 12 UTC, transmitted at about 1315 and 0115 UTC. Covers north-eastern North America, the North Atlantic between 30 and 70 degrees north (including Greenland) and part of western Europe.

Units and map: speeds in knots, heights in hundreds of feet, pressure in hPa, times in UTC. Polar stereographic projection true at 60 degrees north (WMO No. 49 requirement). Background shows provincial, federal and territorial boundaries, oceans, coastlines and major lakes.

Content: surface pressure centres and fronts, areas of significant cloud, turbulence and icing, and freezing levels. Tropical cyclones, volcanic ash and radioactive releases are added when applicable.

Cloud: scalloped outline labelled NCC hh/hh. N is BKN or OVC. CC is the cloud type, or LYR for several layers. hh/hh is the top and base in hundreds of feet ASL. XX means the base is below the 700 hPa level.
Turbulence: a symbol (moderate or severe) with hh/hh top and base. A turbulence forecast means more than 50% chance of encountering turbulence somewhere in the area.
Icing: a symbol (moderate or severe) with hh/hh top and base, XX for a base below 700 hPa.
CB, thunderstorms, TCU and ACC automatically imply moderate or severe turbulence and icing. Where one is forecast, no turbulence or icing symbol is used.
Freezing levels: dashed lines every 5,000 ft, labelled in hundreds of feet ASL.
Pressure centres: L or H with central pressure in hPa. Tropical cyclones: a tropical storm symbol or a filled hurricane symbol with the official name.
Motion: the mean direction and speed (kt) of pressure centres, fronts and trowals is added when the speed is above 5 kt. Values are six-hour means centred on the valid time.

NAV CANADA guide only: Upper-Level Sig Wx covers FL250 to FL600 (400 to 70 mb). Jet stream depth is shown as a plus number (depth above the maximum) and a minus number (depth below). Its symbol list also names thunderstorm, severe line squall, and dust or sand storm, and a CAT or MXD abbreviation under turbulence or icing symbols.
MANAIR gives the mid-level and North Atlantic tops as FL240 (400 hPa). The NAV CANADA guide gives FL250. MANAIR 2024 is treated as the current standard.
The US produces convective SIGMETs and Center Weather Advisories.
The US area forecast (FA) is valid 12 hours with an additional 6-hour outlook and uses a low IFR (LIFR) category: ceilings under 500 ft or visibility under 1 SM.
Transcribed Weather Broadcasts (TWEB) are extensively used in the US.

lesson.note: Always check current SIGMETs and AIRMETs together with the GFA. Both amend it automatically.

terms: Graphic Area Forecast: six charts covering surface to 24,000 ft.
Warning of severe hazards. WS, WV (ash) and WC (tropical cyclone).
Advisory of moderate hazards not already in the GFA.
Observed or forecast status of the phenomenon in a SIGMET or AIRMET.
Winds and temperatures aloft forecast, digital form.
Layers combined when separated by less than 2,000 ft.
GFA coverage: over 50%, over 25% to 50%, 25% or less.

topics.title: MANAIR definitions (Chapter 8)
lesson: MANAIR Chapter 8 defines the terms the manual uses. The manual notes they may not suit general use, so some differ from everyday meaning. This topic paraphrases them. The wording in the manual itself is the reference.

list: TAF and aerodrome advisory: both are in TAF code. An advisory is for aerodromes that do not fully meet ECCC observing standards.
METAR is actual weather at a place and time, normally on the hour. SPECI is issued when a significant change is observed.
GFA: chart forecast of the most probable conditions from the surface to 24,000 ft. SIGMET and AIRMET: MWO messages on specified hazardous weather. An AIRMET covers weather not already in the GFA.
Forecast, prognostic chart and PIREP round out the product terms (see the term list).
Altitude is measured from mean sea level; height is measured from a specified datum such as the ground.
Flight level is hundreds of feet on the 1013.25 hPa (29.92 inHg) datum, so it is not necessarily true altitude.
Canada's AOR is the seven domestic FIRs plus the Gander Oceanic FIR/CTA. A FIR extends upward from the surface; a CTA is controlled airspace extending upward from a specified height.

lesson: Ceiling is the lesser of two heights: the base of the lowest cloud layer whose summation amount is more than 4/8 of the sky, or the vertical visibility in a surface-based layer that completely obscures the sky.

lesson.note: Do not mix up period of validity (the span a forecast covers), period of coverage (the span a TAF program covers daily) and part-period (a segment of the validity period).

list: ECCC: federal department providing meteorological information to Canadians. MSC is its component that provides science, policy and service support, coordinates national standards for the aviation weather program for TC and NAV CANADA, and prepares aviation products for DND.

NAV CANADA: private, non-share capital corporation that owns and runs Canada's civil air navigation system. It is responsible for aviation weather services in Canadian airspace, specifies where and how often observations and forecasts are made, and disseminates them.
Transport Canada (TC): federal regulator of civil aviation. CARs: rules under the Aeronautics Act, in force since 10 October 1996.
DND: department with authority and responsibility to provide and arrange meteorological services for military aviation operations and training.
ICAO: UN specialized agency developing principles and techniques of international air navigation. WMO: UN specialized agency, the UN system's authoritative voice on the atmosphere.
An MWO keeps a continuous watch over its area and is responsible for SIGMET, AIRMET and information on volcanic activity and radioactive release. A CMAC fulfils the MWO role.
CCMEP supplies analyses and NWP guidance to the forecast production centres.
An AMF is a meteorologist meeting the WMO-No. 1083 competency standards for aeronautical meteorology, continuously and actively responsible for the content of an aviation forecast service.

terms: Forecast in TAF code for a designated aerodrome, usually routine: a concise statement of expected conditions for a specified period.
Forecast in TAF code for an aerodrome that does not fully meet ECCC weather observing standards.
Aerodrome routine meteorological report: actual conditions at a place and time as observed from the ground. Normally taken and sent on the hour.
Aviation selected special weather report, issued when a weather change significant to aviation is observed.
Chart-form forecast of the most probable conditions from the surface to 24,000 ft over an area at a specified time.
Message from a meteorological watch office warning of occurring or expected specified weather that may affect aircraft safety, and its development in time and space.
Message from an MWO on specified weather that may affect safety and was not already in the GFA, with its development in time and space.
Forecast of one or more meteorological elements for a specified time or period and surface or airspace, drawn on a chart.
Report by a pilot of weather conditions encountered in flight.

Lesser of: height above ground or water of the base of the lowest cloud layer whose summation amount exceeds half the sky (more than 4/8), or the vertical visibility in a surface-based layer that completely obscures the sky.
Standard nominal altitude in hundreds of feet, calculated from the standard pressure datum 1013.25 hPa (29.92 inHg). Not necessarily true altitude.
Altitude is vertical distance measured from mean sea level. Height is vertical distance from a specified datum, for example the ground. ASL and AGL give feet above sea level or ground level.
Area where Canada provides aviation weather forecast services to civil aviation: the seven domestic FIRs plus the Gander Oceanic FIR/CTA.
Airspace of defined dimensions from the surface upward in which flight information and alerting services are provided.
Controlled airspace extending upward from a specified height above the surface.
Span of time a forecast covers (also valid period). A forecast stays valid only until another forecast, amended or cancelled, is issued for the same area or aerodrome.
Span of time a TAF program covers daily.
A portion or segment of a forecast's period of validity.
English using approved MSC abbreviations from the Manual of Word Abbreviations (MANAB).
Non-abbreviated English in a telegraphic format meant to convey weather information to aviation efficiently.
Meteorological watch office: keeps continuous watch over conditions affecting flight in its area. Responsible for SIGMET and AIRMET and for information on volcanic activity and radioactive release.
Canadian Meteorological Aviation Centre: produces aviation forecasts and monitors conditions affecting flight in Canada. It fulfils the MWO role.
Canadian Centre for Meteorological and Environmental Prediction: the MSC component that assimilates weather data and produces analyses, forecasts and NWP guidance.

topics.title: Aviation weather products and observation programs (NAV CANADA guide)
lesson: The NAV CANADA Aviation Weather Services Guide sorts weather information into alphanumeric data and graphic products, and into current weather (what has occurred) and forecast weather (the most likely future conditions). This topic paraphrases its product tables. Where it differs from MANAIR (2024), MANAIR is treated as the standard.

list: SIGMET: as required, valid up to 4 hours; volcanic ash and tropical cyclone SIGMETs valid 6 hours.
AIRMET: as required, up to 4 hours, valid until updated, cancelled or a new GFA is issued. Covers phenomena up to and including 24,000 ft that were not already in the GFA.
PIREP: when received from a pilot. METAR: on the hour, Canadian. SPECI: when required.
TAF: forecast conditions within 5 nautical miles of the aerodrome. See the CFS for issue times; normally updated every 6 hours, more often at larger airports.

FB (winds and temperatures aloft): low levels 3,000, 6,000, 9,000, 12,000 and 18,000 ft; high levels FL240, 300, 340, 390, 450 and 530. The guide says twice daily from 00Z or 12Z data, valid 24 hours. MANAIR says four times daily from 00, 06, 12 and 18 UTC data, with FBCN31, 33 and 35 as the 6, 12 and 24 hour forecasts.

Space Weather Advisory: event-based, for airspace under NAV CANADA responsibility. It covers GNSS navigation and satellite-based surveillance, HF radio communications, and radiation exposure at FL250 and above.
Surface analysis chart: four times daily, valid 00, 06, 12, 18Z. Covers all of Canada, Alaska and the northern US: MSL pressure, fronts and detailed station plots.

Upper air analysis chart: twice daily, valid 00Z and 12Z. North American coverage at 850 hPa (5,000 ft), 700 hPa (10,000 ft), 500 hPa (18,000 ft) and 250 hPa (34,000 ft): height, wind, temperature and moisture.

GFA: four times daily at 00, 06, 12, 18Z, each valid 12 hours with an additional 12-hour IFR outlook. Seven regional charts, GFACN31 Pacific, 32 Prairies, 33 Ontario/Quebec, 34 Atlantic, 35 Yukon, 36 Nunavut, 37 Arctic. Weather up to and including 24,000 ft, as three Clouds and Weather charts and three Icing, Turbulence and Freezing Level charts.

Local Graphic Forecast (LGF): issued four times daily at 15Z, 18Z, 21Z and 00Z, each valid 6 hours; the last includes an outlook for the next morning. Local coverage of specific areas (for example the West Coast VFR LGF). Depicts weather below 10,000 ft and supplements the GFA.

Significant Weather Prognosis chart: four times daily, valid 00, 06, 12, 18Z. High-level FL250 to 600 (400 to 70 hPa), mid-level FL100 to 250 (700 to 400 hPa), North Atlantic surface to FL250 (SFC to 400 hPa). MANAIR gives FL240 for the mid-level and North Atlantic tops.
Turbulence Forecast chart: moderate and severe turbulence (jet stream and convective) between FL280 and FL430, national and North Atlantic coverage.
Upper Level Wind and Temperature chart: FL240, FL340, FL390 and FL450. Volcanic Ash Forecast chart: as required, depicting the expected ash cloud (plume).

Weather radar imagery: updated every 10 minutes (guide table), composite or single-site, precipitation intensity or echo tops, line of sight within a limited horizontal range. ECCC says its S-band product is produced every 6 minutes.
Satellite imagery: GOES images updated every 30 minutes; POES images about every 6 hours. Infrared and visible.
Weather cameras: images updated every 10 minutes, fixed viewing angles, colour pictures with date and time superimposed and the local METAR shown if available.
Canada has more than 230 surface weather observation sites. Data are collected by a human observer or a suite of automated sensors and coded into observations.
METAR is the routine observation on the hour. SPECI is issued at other times for a significant weather change. If a METAR or SPECI is produced by automated sensors it is marked AUTO in the body.

SAWR (Supplementary Aviation Weather Reporting Station): an aviation weather site that gives additional or limited observations. Unlike a fully staffed station it operates only in specific hours on a reduced schedule.

METAR: taken by qualified human observers. METAR AUTO: taken by a stand-alone AWOS with enhancements; examples are NAV CANADA AWOS and DND AWOS. LWIS: automated hourly report of wind speed, direction, temperature, dew point and altimeter setting. AUTO (system): reports a variety of elements but does not meet the requirements to produce a METAR, SPECI or LWIS report.
WxCam: a NAV CANADA aviation weather camera, images through the CFPS landing page every 10 minutes. Webcam: camera not belonging to NAV CANADA.
Hours of coverage appear as, for example, METAR 09-21Z; 24-hour sites show H24 (METAR H24, METAR AUTO H24, LWIS H24); mixed programs show METAR 12-20Z O/T LWIS.
Some sites broadcast the latest observation by automated voice on VHF; the frequency is in the COMM box (examples given: COMM AWOS 124.7, COMM AUTO 122.025).
AWOS: full suite of sensors for cloud base height, sky cover, visibility, temperature, dew point, wind velocity, altimeter setting, precipitation occurrence, type, amount and intensity, and icing.
LWIS: more basic, measuring only wind, altimeter setting, temperature and dew point. AWOS and LWIS may have a voice generation module.

AWOS enhancements: thunderstorm reporting within the Canadian Lightning Detection Network area; ice-resistant anemometer (AWOS and LWIS); density altitude; laser ceilometer reporting cloud bases up to 25,000 ft; improved obstructions to vision (HZ, BR, FG, FZFG, BLSN); RVR where RVR sensors are installed; remarks when data are missing.
AWOS outside lightning network coverage gets no lightning data, so it cannot report thunderstorm or lightning activity.

AWOS lightning reporting by distance: TS if lightning is detected at 6 SM or less; VCTS if detected from more than 6 to 10 SM; LTNG DIST (with octant direction in remarks, for example LTNG DIST NE, S, SW) if from more than 10 to 30 SM; LTNG DIST ALL QUADS if detected in four or more octants.

CLD MISG sky condition; ICG MISG icing; PCPN MISG precipitation; PRES MISG pressure (altimeter); RVR MISG; T MISG temperature; TD MISG dew point; TS/LTNG TEMPO UNAVBL thunderstorm or lightning data unavailable; VIS MISG; WND MISG; WX MISG weather data.

topics.title: Synoptic code SYNOP (MANOBS Part B)
lesson: The synoptic code (SYNOP) is the international WMO code for surface observations from land stations, staffed or automatic. MANOBS Part B covers it in chapters 14 and 15 and refers to WMO Manual on Codes No. 306. Part B is not a regulatory document used in aviation safety regulations, so changes to it are not put through the Transport Canada consultation process. This topic paraphrases chapters 14 and 15 of MANOBS 8th ed., Amendment 3.

list: Synoptic reports are made at least four times a day, at 0000, 0600, 1200 and 1800 UTC (main synoptic hours). A complete report can hold more than 20 pieces of information, including pressure from barometer readings taken at the same moment worldwide.

The barometer is always read at the hour. All other elements are observed, recorded and coded in the 10 minutes before the hour (start 15 minutes before in difficult weather). Stations follow this schedule unless the ADM gives special permission.
Intermediate synoptic reports are also taken at some stations; their precipitation group covers 3 hours and sits in Section 3.
Six sections numbered 0 to 5, made of five-figure groups. Most groups start with a fixed indicator figure (1, 2, 3 and so on), so omitting one group does not change how the others are identified.

Main Canadian messages normally contain Sections 0, 1 and 3. Section 5 (national daily data) is added once daily to the 0600 UTC message. Section 2 (sea stations) follows MANMAR. Section 4 is not used in Canada.
The message ends with the separation signal = attached to the last group. Missing data are written X and sent as a solidus (/).

Section 0: AAXX identifies a land-station report; YYGGiw is the day, hour and wind indicator; IIiii is the block and station number. The communications computer normally inserts the first two groups. The date of the 0000 UTC report is the day just beginning.
Section 1 order: iR ix h VV, N dd ff, (00fff), 1snTTT, 2snTdTdTd, 3P0P0P0P0, 4PPPP, 5appp, 6RRRtR, 7wwW1W2, 8NhCLCMCH, 9GGgg.
iw (wind indicator): 0 estimated m/s, 1 anemometer m/s, 3 estimated knots, 4 anemometer knots. Canadian land stations use 4 (inserted by the computer).
Block number: Canadian land stations use 71 or 73. The station number comes from METSTAT.

iR (precipitation group indicator): 1 means group 6RRRtR is in Section 1 (main hours); 2 means it is in Section 3 (intermediate hours); 4 means precipitation is not normally measured. Codes 0 and 3 are not used in Canada.
ix (station type): staffed 1 (7-group included), 2 (omitted, nothing significant), 3 (omitted, not observed); automatic 4, 5, 6, 7. Automatic stations currently use 5, 6 or 7.

Inclusion rules in Section 1: iRixhVV, Nddff, 1snTTT, 2snTdTdTd, 3P0, 4PPPP, 5appp and 6RRRtR are always included (5appp whenever the 3-hour tendency is available). 00fff only if wind is 99 kt or more. 7wwW1W2 only if significant present or past weather was observed. 8NhCLCMCH only if cloud was observed.

lesson.h: Height, visibility, cloud and wind groups

list: h: base of the lowest cloud, in code figures 0 to 9 (0 is under 50 m, 4 is 300 to under 600 m, 9 is above 2500 m or no cloud). / means sky completely obscured. If only CH cloud is present, h is 9.

VV: code figures for visibility (00 is 0, 16 is 1 mile, 48 is 3, 58 is 5, 59 is 6, 74 is 15). If the visibility falls between two code figures, use the lower: 20 miles is 80, 30 miles is 83. When an hourly and a synoptic observation are taken together and prevailing visibility is 15+, VV is 74. Codes 90 to 99 only on special instruction from the ADM.

N: total cloud in oktas. 7 means 7 oktas or more but not 8; 9 means sky completely obscured; / means indiscernible or not observed. Cloud seen through partial obscuration is counted as though the obscuration did not exist. A mackerel sky (AC or SC perlucidus) is at most 7.
dd: 10-minute mean wind direction from true north in tens of degrees: 00 calm, 09 east, 18 south, 27 west, 36 north.

ff: 10-minute mean speed in knots. At 99 kt or more, ff is 99 and the extra group 00fff gives the actual speed (an east wind of 118 kt is N0999 00118). The conversion table from mph to knots (10 mph is 9 kt, 34 mph is 30 kt) is not reversible.

1snTTT and 2snTdTdTd: sn is 0 for 0 C or above and 1 for below 0; the value is the absolute temperature in tenths of a degree. Examples: 15.3 C is 10153; -15.3 C is 11153; -0.9 C is 11009; 0.0 C is 10000; dew point -10.0 is 21100.
3P0P0P0P0 (main reports only): station-level pressure. Below 1000.0 hPa code it directly (987.2 is 39872). At 1000.0 or above, drop the thousands digit (1012.4 is 30124).
4PPPP: mean sea-level pressure in tenths of hPa, same rule (996.2 is 49962; 1015.4 is 40154).

5appp: 3-hour tendency. a is the characteristic (0 to 8; 4 steady; 0 to 3 pressure now same or higher than 3 hours ago; 5 to 8 same or lower), ppp the net change in tenths of hPa (11.2 is 112; 9.3 is 093; 0.8 is 008).

RRR: 000 is 0 mm; 001 to 988 are whole millimetres; 989 is 989 mm or more; 990 is trace; 992 to 999 are 0.2 to 0.9 mm (991 is not used in Canada); /// is not measured. Amounts above 1.0 mm are rounded to the nearest whole millimetre.

tR: duration of the period. 1 is 6 hours (always at stations making main observations every 6 hours), 2 is 12, 3 is 18, 4 is 24, 5 is 1 hour, 6 is 2, 7 is 3, 8 is 9 and 9 is 15 hours. Intermediate reports use 5 to 9.
Main hours put the group in Section 1 (iR 1). Intermediate hours put it in Section 3 (iR 2).

ww covers phenomena occurring at observation time or in the preceding 60 minutes (thunder up to 75 minutes). Codes 00 to 49 are used when no precipitation is occurring at the station; 50 to 99 when it is. The first digit is one of ten categories.

If more than one ww code applies, choose the highest, except that 17 is preferred over 20 to 49. Codes 20 to 27 and 29 are never used when precipitation is occurring at the station. In MANOBS, slight means light.

Key codes: 13 lightning seen, no thunder; 17 thunder heard within 15 minutes, no precipitation at the station; 19 funnel cloud, waterspout or tornado (for a tornado, the plain word TORNADO is the last group of Section 3); 29 thunderstorm in the preceding hour but none now; 95 thunderstorm with rain or snow; 96 thunderstorm with hail or snow pellets. Codes 97 and 99 are no longer used in Canada.

Drizzle, rain and snow: 50 and 51 slight drizzle (intermittent, continuous), 60 and 61 slight rain, 62 and 63 moderate rain, 64 and 65 heavy rain, 70 to 75 snow, 80 to 82 rain showers, 85 and 86 snow showers. Freezing rain is 66 (slight) and 67 (moderate or heavy).
A thunderstorm is in progress at the station when thunder is heard in the 15 minutes before the observation, or overhead lightning is seen in that time and noise might prevent hearing thunder.

W1W2 (past weather): 0, 1, 2 describe cloud amount (N 4 or less; more than half part of the period; more than half throughout), 3 sandstorm, dust storm or blowing snow, 4 fog, 5 drizzle, 6 rain, 7 snow, 8 showers, 9 thunderstorm. The period normally runs from the previous synoptic observation to when the present weather began, at most 6 hours at main hours. W1 differs from ww where possible. If there was a break in the weather watch over 30 minutes, W1W2 may be XX.
The 8-group is omitted when the sky is clear (N = 0) or completely obscured with no cloud visible.
Nh is the total amount of CL cloud, or of CM cloud if there is no CL; if only CH is present, Nh is 0. There is no height limit: convective cloud based at 12,000 ft still counts as CL.

CL priority: if cumulonimbus is present, CL is 9 when the top of at least one is clearly fibrous or striated, otherwise 3. Without cumulonimbus the order is 4 (stratocumulus formed by spreading cumulus), 8, 2, then 1, 5, 6 or 7 by which type predominates.
9GGgg gives the actual observation time when it differs by more than 10 minutes from the scheduled hour GG.
Always included in Canadian land-station reports. Main reports always carry 333, 1snTxTxTx (maximum temperature), 2snTnTnTn (minimum) and 7R24R24R24R24 (24-hour precipitation).
Maximum temperature: at 1200 UTC the 24-hour maximum ending 6 hours earlier (0600); at 1800 and 0000 UTC the previous 12 hours; at 0600 UTC the previous 24 hours.
Minimum temperature: at 1200 UTC the previous 12 hours; at 1800 and 0600 UTC the previous 24 hours; at 0000 UTC the previous 18 hours.

4E'sss: state of the ground and depth of snow or ice, included when solid precipitation is on the ground and precipitation has occurred since the last main report (and at 1200 UTC whenever it is on the ground). Ice from freezing precipitation alone is excluded. E' 0 to 9 describes cover (7 is an even layer of loose dry snow covering the ground). sss is whole centimetres: 997 is trace (under 0.5 cm), 998 is snow cover not continuous.
7R24: tenths of mm for the 24 hours. Nil is 70000, trace 79999, 25.3 mm is 70253, 999.8 mm or more is 79998.

Special groups: 909Rtdc gives when precipitation began or ended (Rt) and its duration and character (dc), used whenever 6RRRtR is coded and RRR is not 000; 931ss gives the depth of newly fallen snow in whole centimetres (up to 55; at the Regional Director General's discretion, four staffed observations a day, 1 cm or more).

Rt: 1 is less than 1 hour ago, 2 is 1 to 2 hours, up to 6 for 5 to 6 hours, 7 is 6 to 12 hours, 8 is more than 12 hours, 9 unknown. dc: 0 to 3 for one period of precipitation (under 1 hour, 1 to 3, 3 to 6, over 6 hours) and 4 to 7 for two or more periods. Periods separated by 15 minutes or more count as separate.
Sent once daily as the last section of the 0600 UTC message, for the 24 hours ending at 0600 UTC.
1ssss: snowfall in tenths of cm (0.6 cm is 10006; trace 19999; none 10000; not measured 1////). 2swswswsw: water equivalent of the snowfall in tenths of mm (trace 29999; none 20000).

3dmdmfmfm: direction and speed of the maximum wind, reported only when it exceeds 16 kt (mean or gust). 4fhftftfi: hundreds digit, time of occurrence and speed range of the maximum two-minute mean: 0 is 16 kt or less, 1 is 17 to 27, 2 is 28 to 33, 3 is 34 kt or more.
